implementation_notes: Scala 2.13 ships the guard in the standard library: Using.resource(resource)(body) runs the body and releases the resource even if it throws, Using(resource)(body) wraps the same thing in a Try, Using.resources(...) covers up to four resources releasing them in reverse order, and Using.Manager composes a dynamic number of them; an implicit Releasable instance is provided for every java.lang.AutoCloseable, while other resource types need an explicit Releasable or a wrapper. try/finally remains the substitute for plain non-resource actions. The classic guard object is only justified where the release action must be composed into a larger lifecycle - an effect Resource, a framework hook - rather than one lexical scope.
code_sketch:
import scala.util.Using

val lines: Seq[String] =
  Using.resource(new BufferedReader(new FileReader("file.txt"))) { r =>
    Iterator.continually(r.readLine()).takeWhile(_ != null).toSeq
  }   // released on normal exit and on failure; both errors are suppressed
pitfalls: Using.resource throws whereas Using.apply returns Try: mixing the two (calling .get on the result, ignoring a Failure) loses the release error that was suppressed behind the primary one.

Only AutoCloseable gets an implicit Releasable, so a handshake that returns a handle plus a state object needs its own Releasable instance - wrapping the wrong object compiles and releases the wrong thing.

In effect-based code a Resource value that is never `use`d performs neither acquisition nor release, and release order is reverse of acquire with non-interruptible acquire/release in cats-effect - a stronger but different guarantee than the stdlib's.

variants.name: cats-effect Resource / bracket (effect-typed guard)
variants.implementation_notes: In effect-typed code the guard becomes a first-class value: Resource.make(acquire)(release) describes the lifecycle, `use` runs the action and guarantees finalization, `bracket` is the raw form, and resources compose (>>, both) with release happening in reverse order of acquisition; acquire and release are non-interruptible and finalization happens as soon as the use block finishes, even when the caller is cancelled, which is stronger than the synchronous stdlib Using. Choose this variant when the code is already tagless/effect-based and cleanup must survive cancellation; it costs a cats-effect dependency and requires the resource to be modelled as F[A].
pitfalls: A Resource that is never consumed with `use` performs no cleanup and no acquisition - forgetting to run it compiles and silently leaks nothing (the guard simply never exists).

Because acquire and release are non-interruptible, a resource with unbounded cleanup time makes cancellation wait; choose the stdlib Using for scope-local, uninterruptible-synchronous cleanup instead.
